completeness.repository_coverage: All non-test source under src/Conduit/ read: features handlers, infrastructure, Program.cs, ServicesExtensions.cs, domain. Tests, build scripts and realworld/ not reviewed in depth.

unknowns.subject: Production database provider, data volumes and concurrency
unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: Deployment config, row counts, and a load test with thread-pool counters

unknowns.subject: Actual SQL emitted and query plans
unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: EF Core query log and EXPLAIN against a seeded database

known: Default provider is SQLite with a local file (Program.cs:15-16); SqlServer is selectable in code
Every request passes a transaction pipeline behavior (ServicesExtensions.cs:26)
No HasIndex declarations exist in the model
No metrics, tracing, benchmarks or load tests are in the repository
unknown: Row counts for articles, persons, tags, comments
assumed: Findings that depend on data volume or concurrency are capped at Medium or rely on stated conditions (PERF-001, PERF-002, PERF-003, PERF-006)
derived: Rows per listed article = favorites x tags from the two sibling collection Includes (PERF-004)

root_causes.description: Synchronous database calls inside async request paths
Hot lookup keys without declared indexes
Article list query is unbounded and over-fetches
Unbounded collection reads for comments and tags
Whole follow collections loaded to test membership
Per-item round trips in article creation

findings.problem: The mediator pipeline behavior wrapping every request calls the synchronous BeginTransaction() and CommitTransaction() (Database.BeginTransaction, IDbContextTransaction.Commit) inside an async handler, blocking a thread-pool thread on database round trips for every request.
findings.performance_principle: Do not hold a shared worker thread across I/O; use the non-blocking form so threads serve other requests while waiting.

evidence.statement: Behavior calls context.BeginTransaction() and context.CommitTransaction() synchronously around await next().
BeginTransaction() calls Database.BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted) and CommitTransaction() calls _currentTransaction?.Commit(); BeginTransactionAsync/CommitAsync exist.
Behavior is registered through AddMediator PipelineBehaviors, so it applies to every query and command, including read-only GETs.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Matters when the SqlServer provider is used (selectable in Program.cs; default is SQLite) and concurrent requests exceed the thread-pool minimum so continuations queue behind blocked threads. On in-process SQLite the cost is small. Production provider and concurrency are unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for async transaction use or a transaction-less read path; none. Begin is skipped only for the InMemory provider.
Default provider is SQLite, where blocking cost is much lower; deployed provider unknown, so impact on SqlServer is unverified.

findings.recommendation: Use BeginTransactionAsync and CommitAsync/RollbackAsync with the cancellation token in the behavior, and consider skipping the transaction for read-only queries.
findings.trade_offs: Transaction methods on ConduitContext become async; read-only requests without a transaction lose snapshot consistency across their multiple queries.

validation.metric: ThreadPool Queue Length and Thread Count (dotnet-counters) and p99 latency of GET /api/articles under concurrent load
validation.expectation: Queue length stays near zero at a concurrency where the blocking version grows it; direction only, magnitude unmeasured.
validation.falsifier: No thread-pool queue growth or latency difference between sync and async versions at target concurrency on the production provider.
validation.guard: Review rule or analyzer flagging synchronous EF Core calls in handlers.

commands.purpose: Observe ThreadPool Queue Length and Thread Count during a load test

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If production runs SQLite or low concurrency, the blocked window is tiny and the pool never starves.

alternatives.why: Removes the blocking call at its source with no semantic change.
Masks starvation instead of removing the blocking work.

alternatives.option: Skip the transaction for read queries
alternatives.why: Complementary; saves round trips but does not fix commands.

findings.problem: The article list handler computes ArticlesCount with synchronous IQueryable.Count() at the end of an async handler, blocking a thread and issuing a second query that re-applies all Includes.
findings.performance_principle: Do not hold a shared worker thread across I/O.

evidence.statement: ArticlesCount = queryable.Count(); queryable still carries the GetAllData() Includes plus filters.
The same handler uses ToListAsync elsewhere, so the sync call is inconsistent rather than forced.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: GET /api/articles and /api/articles/feed under concurrency above the thread-pool minimum with a non-trivial articles table; both are unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for a cheaper count (cached or denormalized); none.
Count over a small table is fast, which bounds the blocked window.

findings.recommendation: Use CountAsync(cancellationToken) on a query without the Includes, sharing the filter predicates.
findings.trade_offs: Filter predicates must be shared between the page and count queries to stay consistent.

validation.metric: SQL emitted for GET /api/articles (query log) and thread-pool queue length under load
validation.expectation: Count query has no joins to ArticleFavorites/ArticleTags and no sync call remains.
validation.falsifier: Count time is negligible against total request time at realistic table size.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: A single count query is short on small data; blocked time equals its duration only.

alternatives.option: CountAsync on a query without Includes
alternatives.why: Removes blocking and join work together.

findings.problem: Lookup keys used on hot paths (Article.Slug, Person.Username, Person.Email) have no declared index or unique constraint; EF Core indexes only foreign keys by convention, so these filters likely scan their tables.
findings.performance_principle: Frequent equality predicates need an access path so cost does not grow linearly with table size.

evidence.statement: Slug is a plain property with no index; it is the lookup key in Details, Edit, Delete, Comments, Favorites and the uniqueness probe loops.
OnModelCreating configures composite keys and conversions only; no HasIndex.
Authenticated handlers resolve the user with Persons.FirstOrDefaultAsync(x => x.Username == ...) (Favorites Add, Articles Create, ProfileReader).
Login filters Persons by Email; Users Create probes Username and Email.
Schema is created with EnsureCreated and the repository holds no migrations, so the model is the only index source.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Matters once Articles and Persons grow beyond what is cheap to scan; row counts are unknown. Each authenticated request adds a Username scan.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched all .cs files for HasIndex and [Index]; none. No generated schema seen, so an index added out of band cannot be ruled out.
Slug uniqueness is not enforced by the database either, so the probe loops are racy (correctness note).

findings.recommendation: Declare unique indexes on Article.Slug, Person.Username and Person.Email in OnModelCreating and provide a way to apply them to existing databases.
findings.trade_offs: Insert overhead; unique constraints can fail on existing duplicates; EnsureCreated will not alter an existing database, so a migration path is needed.

validation.metric: Query plan for lookups by Slug and Username
validation.expectation: Plan changes from SCAN to SEARCH using an index; direction only.
validation.falsifier: Plan already shows an index search because an index was created out of band.

commands.command: sqlite3 realworld.db "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM Articles WHERE Slug = 'x';"
commands.purpose: Check whether the Slug lookup scans or uses an index on the default SQLite database

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: The sample app is typically small; with a few thousand rows the scans are cheap.

alternatives.why: Fixes lookup cost and enforces the uniqueness the handlers assume.
Adds invalidation; an index is cheaper.

findings.problem: The article list takes a client-supplied limit with no cap, uses OFFSET pagination, joins two sibling collections (ArticleFavorites and ArticleTags) in one query, and fetches Body that is then nulled in memory.
findings.performance_principle: Bound result size and per-item fan-out; do not transfer data that is discarded.

evidence.statement: Take(message.Limit ?? 20) with no maximum; limit and offset come straight from the query string.
GetAllData includes Author, ArticleFavorites and ArticleTags: two sibling collection Includes in one statement multiply rows per article.
Body is loaded then set to null for every article before serialization.
Favorites are loaded as full rows only so FavoritesCount can be computed from list length.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: A caller sending a large limit, articles with many favorites and tags (rows per article = favorites x tags, derived from the join shape), or deep offsets on a large table; none of these volumes is known.

counter_evidence.statement: Default page is 20, which bounds the common case.
Searched for a global maximum page size or filter; none found.

findings.recommendation: Clamp limit to a documented maximum, project to a DTO that excludes Body and uses a favorite count, and avoid the double collection join (split query or subqueries); consider keyset pagination if deep offsets matter.
findings.trade_offs: Projection changes how the entity is serialized; the clamp changes behavior for clients requesting large pages.

validation.metric: Rows and bytes returned by the list SQL for an article with many favorites and tags
validation.expectation: Rows per page drop from a product to one per article; direction only.
validation.falsifier: Query log shows no row multiplication at realistic favorite and tag counts.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: With the default limit and typical favorite and tag counts the row multiplication is modest.

alternatives.option: Clamp limit and project to a DTO with counts
alternatives.why: Removes transferred data and fan-out at the source.
Avoids the product but still loads Body and full favorite rows.

findings.problem: GET comments loads the article with all comments and each comment author, tracked and unpaged; GET tags loads the whole Tags table per request.
findings.performance_principle: Work and response size per request must not grow without bound with data.

evidence.statement: Articles.Include(Comments).ThenInclude(Author).FirstOrDefaultAsync with change tracking and no limit.
Tags.OrderBy(TagId).AsNoTracking().ToListAsync() with no limit and no caching.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Articles with large comment threads, or a tag table grown by user-created tags; sizes unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: The RealWorld spec returns all comments and tags unpaged, which limits how far this can change.
Searched for caching of tags; none.

findings.recommendation: Add AsNoTracking and projection to the comments query; cap or briefly cache the tags response if the table grows.
findings.trade_offs: A tags cache introduces short staleness.

validation.metric: Query time and response size of GET /api/tags and of comments for a large article
validation.expectation: Tracking overhead removed; size unchanged unless capped.
validation.falsifier: Counts stay in the tens so cost is negligible.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Spec compliance requires returning all comments and tags; with small tables the cost is trivial.

alternatives.option: AsNoTracking plus projection; cap or cache tags

findings.problem: Follow checks load whole collections: ReadProfile includes both Following and Followers of the current user to test one id (Following is unused); the feed and list handlers load the full followed-id list.
findings.performance_principle: Test membership in the database instead of transferring the whole set.

evidence.statement: Persons.Include(Following).Include(Followers) then Followers.Any(x => x.TargetId == person.PersonId).
Feed loads Persons.Include(Followers), then queries over Followers.Select(TargetId).Contains.
All followed ids are loaded into a list for every authenticated list request.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Authenticated users who follow or are followed by many accounts; counts are unknown (Medium confidence because of this assumption).

counter_evidence.statement: Follow counts per user are likely modest in a sample app, which bounds impact.

findings.recommendation: Use AnyAsync on FollowedPeople with observer and target ids, drop the unused Following include, and query follow state only for authors on the returned page.

validation.metric: Rows materialized per request for authenticated GET /api/profiles/{username} and /api/articles (query log)
validation.falsifier: Follow counts of a few dozen make the difference unmeasurable.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: A typical user follows tens of accounts; loading them costs little.

alternatives.why: Cost becomes independent of follow count.

findings.problem: Article creation does sequential per-tag round trips (FindAsync, plus an immediate SaveChanges per new tag) and an AnyAsync probe per slug collision, inside the request transaction.
findings.performance_principle: Batch dependent writes; avoid per-item round trips inside a held transaction.

evidence.statement: foreach tag: FindAsync, then AddAsync and SaveChangesAsync for each new tag.
Slug uniqueness loop issues one AnyAsync per collision suffix.
No runtime evidence (profile, trace, load test, EXPLAIN) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Create requests with many tags or many same-title articles; writes are rarer than reads and tag lists are small.

counter_evidence.statement: Tag lists are typically a handful, which bounds the loop.

findings.recommendation: Fetch existing tags with one Contains query and save once; find colliding slugs with one prefix query.
findings.trade_offs: A single SaveChanges changes handling of concurrent tag creation (duplicate-key race).

validation.metric: SQL statements per POST /api/articles with N tags
validation.falsifier: N is small and writes are rare.

considered_not_reported.observation: PasswordHasher uses a single HMAC-SHA512 pass and a shared HMACSHA512 instance
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Cheap CPU work, not a performance bottleneck; the weak key derivation is a security matter (adjacent finding)
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Password hashing is changed to a deliberately slow KDF, which would need offloading from request threads

considered_not_reported.observation: Serilog configured at Verbose minimum level writing to console
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Log volume per request unknown and no per-request logging calls found in handlers
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Production logs show high volume or framework categories at Debug/Trace

adjacent_findings.problem: The JWT signing key and password-hash HMAC key are hard-coded in source, and passwords are hashed with one fast HMAC-SHA512 pass.

evidence.statement: Signing key literal in AddJwt.
HMAC key literal and single-pass hash.

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Load keys from secret configuration and use a purpose-built password hash (PBKDF2/Argon2) with per-user salt cost.
